chief_complaint: pain on thumb side of wrist when gripping, positive Finkelstein
hpi_details: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain on thumb side of wrist when gripping, positive finkelstein. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she developed wear-and-tear arthritis or sprained a small ligament at the base of her thumb from excessive typing and phone use.
concerns: She is worried that the stabbing pain will become so severe that she will keep dropping cookware and eventually need surgery on her hand.
expectations: She hopes to receive a cortisone injection or a thumb brace so she can pinch and grip without sharp pain.

clinical_knowledge.topic: De Quervain tenosynovitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of De Quervain tenosynovitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for De Quervain Tenosynovitis: Thumb spica splint, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Carpal tunnel syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

red_flags: New weakness, persistent numbness, marked swelling after trauma, fever, or a red hot wrist requires assessment for another diagnosis or infection.

must_ask.objective: Characterize the pain location and triggers
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does gripping or twisting make it worse?
Do you do a lot of repetitive gripping, like lifting a baby or using tools?
How long has this been bothering you?
Have you tried anything for this pain already?

must_ask.objective: Explain the splint and injection treatment
must_ask.say: We'll start with a thumb spica splint and anti-inflammatory medication, with a steroid injection as an option if needed.

history.answer: My right wrist hurts right by the base of my thumb, especially whenever I try to grip something or pinch my fingers together.
It is only on the thumb side of my right wrist; my left wrist and all my other joints feel completely normal.
It started about two weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse over the last few days.
It feels like an annoying ache at rest, but it turns into a sharp, catching pain whenever I move my thumb. On a scale of one to ten, it reaches about a six when it flares up.
Pinching my thumb, twisting open jars, wringing towels, or lifting a heavy pan triggers a sharp shooting pain right away.
Resting my hand and keeping my thumb completely still helps ease the throbbing.
I do a lot of repetitive typing and mouse work at my office job, and over the past month I have also been doing heavy yard work and potting plants at home.
There is a little bit of puffiness right over the bone near the base of my thumb, but no redness and it does not feel hot.
My wrist feels slightly stiff for five to ten minutes when I first get out of bed, but it quickly loosens up once I start moving around.
It has been hard to turn door handles, hold a coffee mug, or chop vegetables because gripping causes so much discomfort.
No, I have not felt any numbness, pins and needles, or tingling in my hand or fingers.
No, I never fell, hit my wrist, or heard any pop; the pain just built up on its own.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I have never had wrist or thumb pain like this before.
I have been feeling unusually tired and run-down lately, but I have not had any fevers or lost any weight.
No, I have not had any skin rashes, mouth ulcers, hair thinning, or dry eyes and dry mouth.
No, I do not have any lower back pain in the morning, heel tenderness, or swelling in my whole fingers.
No, I have not had any diarrhea, pain when urinating, vaginal discharge, or sore throats recently.
I eat a normal balanced diet, do not eat heavy amounts of organ meats or seafood, and do not take any water pills.
No, I have never had steroid injections, joint aspirations, or any kind of surgery on my joints.
I have been married for fifteen years in a monogamous relationship, and neither of us has any other partners.
I put an ice pack on it a couple of times and tried to rest it over the weekend, but I have not taken any pain relievers or worn a brace yet.

I use my phone and laptop constantly, so I assumed I strained a ligament or developed early arthritis at the base of my thumb. I'm afraid the stabbing pain will get so bad that I'll keep dropping pots and pans, and that I might end up needing hand surgery.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or any autoimmune conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, just a daily multivitamin.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or food.
I have never smoked cigarettes. I only have an occasional glass of wine when out with friends, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an administrative assistant doing computer work, and I live with my husband and daughter.
No one in my family has rheumatoid arthritis, gout, lupus, or other joint problems.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last one was two weeks ago, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and comfortable at rest, holding her right wrist protectively with no acute distress.

Point tenderness and mild localized swelling over the right radial styloid; sharp pain elicited with ulnar deviation of the wrist while clasping the thumb in a closed fist (positive Finkelstein test); first carpometacarpal joint grind test is negative.
No rash, erythema, warmth, nail pitting, or tophi over the hands, wrists, or other joints.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is completely intact throughout the bilateral radial, median, and ulnar nerve distributions; Tinel sign and Phalen maneuver at the carpal tunnel are negative.
Motor strength is 5/5 in bilateral thumb abduction, finger extension, and wrist flexion and extension without thenar or hypothenar atrophy.
Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and capillary refill is under two seconds in all digits.
